title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
population: Endurance athletes (14 studies) with pre-post taper outcomes
findings: 14 studies included; time-trial performance improved (SMD = -0.45; P < 0.05) and time to exhaustion improved (SMD = 1.28; P < 0.05).
No improvements in VO2max or economy of movement (P > 0.05) between pre- and post-tapering.
Tapering combined with pre-taper overload training had a more significant effect on time-trial performance than conventional tapering (P < 0.05).

A taper reducing volume 41-60%, maintaining intensity and frequency, lasting <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days, with a progressive or step pattern, significantly improved time-trial performance (P < 0.05). Authors conclude a <=21-day taper with progressive 41-60% volume reduction without changing intensity or frequency is effective.
limitations: Only 14 studies, mostly small; the abstract does not show that duration subgroups differ from each other; no recreational-runner or ultra data in the abstract; overload-then-taper conclusion rests on few studies; total participants not stated.
implications: Supports a flexible taper window of 7 to 21 days; use 14 days as default and shorten to 7-10 days for short races (5-10 km) or low-volume plans.
Confirms 41-60% volume reduction with intensity and frequency kept; step tapers also worked here, so a step schedule is a valid simpler fallback.
Do not present a taper as a fitness gain: VO2max and economy did not improve; frame it as fatigue dissipation.
A preceding overload block may add benefit, but see aubry-2014-overreaching-before-taper for the functional overreaching caveat.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (PLOS ONE, 10 May 2023, Wang first author). Abstract re-read; findings match. Population for the review is 'endurance athletes', no further breakdown stated.
